A campfire is legal only when there is no fire ban for the district, the land manager allows fires at that site and you keep to the size and clearance rules. Each state runs its own system: NSW, Victoria, South Australia, Western Australia, Tasmania and the ACT declare Total Fire Bans, Queensland declares local fire bans instead, and the Northern Territory's fire bans usually last up to 24 hours.
The rules by state

Solid fuel is the constant: on any ban day, wood, charcoal and heat-bead fires are illegal in the affected district, fire rings included. What changes from state to state is the fire season, the size and clearance rules for a legal fire, and whether a gas cooker is still allowed in a park on a ban day.

campfires-camping-australia.en: The Australian Fire Danger Rating System has four levels, Moderate, High, Extreme and Catastrophic, published by district. A Total Fire Ban is declared separately, so check both rather than reading the rating as permission.

On a ban day, campfires and solid-fuel barbecues are illegal in the district. Gas is where the states differ: NSW national parks generally ban visitor-owned gas cookers, ACT parks switch off gas barbecues, South Australian park rules are set park by park, Tasmania allows LPG and electric stoves but not liquid-fuel ones, and Queensland allows contained gas and spirit stoves during a fire ban.
Parks also close on the worst days. South Australian parks and ForestrySA forests may close on ban days, and NPWS can declare its own park fire ban or close a park in NSW when the risk is high.

Size and clearance rules differ: NSW state forests require a fire under one square metre and 4.5 metres from the nearest tree, Victorian state forests one under a metre across with three metres cleared, and South Australia a trench 30 cm deep during the fire season.

Lighting a fire on a Total Fire Ban day in NSW brings an on-the-spot fine of $2,200, or up to $5,500 and 12 months in jail in court. Western Australia issues a $1,000 infringement, with up to $25,000 and 12 months in jail on conviction.

CFA warns that a fire on a Total Fire Ban day in Victoria can bring a fine of more than $40,000, two years in prison or both. In the Northern Territory, lighting a fire for anything other than cooking without a permit carries up to about $77,000 or five years, and failing to clear 4 metres around a fire up to about $15,000; the amounts are indexed, so check the NT page.

Australian national park camping in 2026 runs from free to more than $40 a night at the busiest serviced sites, such as Tidal River at Wilsons Promontory: Queensland charges $7.75 per person, Western Australia and the Northern Territory $10 to $20 per adult, Victoria's half-price bookable campgrounds start at $16 a site, and some NSW campgrounds charge nothing beyond a $6 booking fee. Take two adults and two children aged 8 and 10 for three nights. A Queensland national park campsite costs $93 at the $31 family rate, a Western Australian campground with basic facilities costs $120 ($15 per adult and $5 per child each night), and a Northern Territory Category A campground costs $114 at the $38 family rate.

A Victorian bookable site from $16 a night comes to about $48 for the same three nights, because Victoria charges per site rather than per person. The order flips for a solo traveller, who pays $23.25 in Queensland and $45 at the same WA campground.

No, the ACT has no free camping: vehicle-based camping is only allowed at established campgrounds, each one needs a booking and charges a fee, and camping on other public land without a permit carries up to 20 penalty units. Bushwalkers can camp in remote parts of Namadgi National Park. AussieCamps maps seven ACT Parks campgrounds and the territory's public dump point.

Parks ACT lists every bookable place to stay in one place: Cotter, Honeysuckle, Orroral, Mount Clear, Woods Reserve, Blue Range, Kowen, Nil Desperandum at Tidbinbilla, Ready-Cut Cottage and the walk-in Northern Border Campground. Bookings must be made in advance and fees apply.

Woods Reserve in Namadgi is closed until early 2027 for a full upgrade, so plan a Namadgi night around Honeysuckle, Orroral or Mount Clear instead (Mount Clear is unsuitable for campervans and caravans, and Orroral is not suitable for large groups).

Namadgi protects 106,095 hectares, almost half of the ACT, and entry is free. Honeysuckle, Orroral and Mount Clear take bookings of up to seven consecutive days and ban motorised generators, and at Honeysuckle you bring your own drinking water.

Bushwalkers can camp in remote parts of Namadgi, and the Namadgi National Park Brief Guide shows the walk-in options. Leave your route with someone, because much of the park sits a long way from help.

The ACT bushfire season runs from 1 October to 31 March unless the ESA Commissioner varies it. Burning off in the open during the season needs a permit, and so do open-air cooking fires on unleased Territory land in rural areas at any time of year.

On a Total Fire Ban day there are no fires in the open. You may use your own gas barbecue or portable gas or liquid-fuel stove in an ACT park on other days, but not on a Total Fire Ban day, and public gas barbecues are switched off.
Kowen Forest's campground sits behind locked gates and may close during fire danger periods or heavy rain, so check the booking conditions before you drive out.

Tidbinbilla Nature Reserve is within an easy drive of the city, and Nil Desperandum there is one of the bookable places to stay in the ACT's parks.
Canberra's national institutions, including the Australian War Memorial and the National Gallery of Australia, have free general admission, which makes a wet day in the city easy to fill.

camping-rules-new-south-wales.en: Camping Rules NSW 2026: Free Camping, State Forests & Fees
Free camp in NSW state forests for up to four weeks. Most national park sites need a booking, $6 even when camping is free. 2026 fire bans and fines.

Yes, you can free camp in New South Wales: every state forest except Cumberland and Strickland allows free, first-come camping for up to four weeks, and some national park campgrounds charge no camping fee, although most of those still take a $6 booking fee. AussieCamps maps 372 NSW national park campgrounds, 869 roadside rest areas and 347 public dump points.

NSW national parks have more than 365 campgrounds, and most of those listed on the NSW National Parks website need a booking even when camping is free; those free sites charge a $6 booking fee. A few basic listed sites, such as Tuross River campground in Wadbilliga National Park, need no booking, and remote camping at unlisted sites needs none either, though NPWS recommends a trip intention form.

Camping fees and park entry are separate. Vehicle entry fees apply at 45 of the more than 890 parks and reserves, such as $8 a day at Myall Lakes and Murramarang, and a booking covers only the number of people specified and paid for: NPWS can charge for, or turn away, extra occupants.

Official advice on rest areas is mixed. Service NSW says rest areas are not for camping, while the July 2026 planning practice note says camping in one may be permitted unless a council or Transport for NSW has put up a no camping or no overnight stays sign.

Camping outside a caravan park or camping ground usually needs council approval unless an exemption in the Local Government Regulation applies, and councils can ban camping on their land with signs. The fine for ignoring a council sign is set by state law at $110 on the spot, and Crown reserves follow the rules of their Crown land manager.
Read the rest area sign
Use car bays, not truck bays
Off-site camping needs council approval

Check the NSW RFS fire danger rating, NPWS park alerts and any park fire ban before you light anything. NPWS can declare a park fire ban or close a park when the fire risk is high, separate from a Total Fire Ban.

In national parks, light fires only in designated fireplaces, never break branches or collect fallen timber, and never run a generator during a fire ban. Not every park allows campfires, so check before you go.

NSW camping rules depend on who manages the land. National Parks and Wildlife Service runs the parks, Forestry Corporation of NSW runs the state forests, councils manage their own land, and Crown land managers look after Crown reserves.
camping-rules-new-south-wales.oldEn: NSW camping rules depend on who manages the land. National parks, state forests, councils and private campgrounds each set their own conditions.

camping-rules-new-south-wales.en: In a state forest you can pitch a tent almost anywhere except on roads, in picnic or permit areas, in pine plantations or in closed forest. Sites cannot be booked, the maximum stay is four weeks unless a sign says less, and many forests have no bins, so take rubbish home.

In a national park you must camp in an area set aside for camping, unless the park allows remote camping, and for no more than 21 days in a row unless a park sign or the plan of management sets a different limit. Camping anywhere else in a park carries a maximum penalty of 30 penalty units.

Parks: 21 days unless signs say otherwise
Councils decide where camping is banned

Popular coastal campgrounds can book out over summer and school holidays, so book as soon as your dates are fixed. The camping fee is charged in full at the time of booking, plus a non-refundable booking fee.
Cancelling 31 days or more before arrival refunds 75% of the fee, and cancelling later refunds 50%. Neither refund includes the booking fee.

The All Parks Pass costs $190 a year and covers vehicle entry at all 45 fee-collecting parks, including Kosciuszko, with restrictions at Chowder Bay and the Cape Byron lighthouse precinct, but no annual pass covers camping. Kosciuszko entry is $29 per 24 hours from the June long weekend to the October long weekend and $17 for the rest of the year.

The statutory Bush Fire Danger Period runs from 1 October to 31 March, although local conditions can change it. During it, the RFS decides each afternoon whether to declare a Total Fire Ban for the next day, and a ban can also be declared on the day itself.

On a Total Fire Ban day you cannot light a fire in the open or use a solid-fuel barbecue, and lighting a fire brings an on-the-spot fine of $2,200, or up to $5,500 and 12 months in jail if it goes to court. In national parks, visitor-owned gas and electric cookers are generally banned too, except inside a caravan or its three-sided annexe.

State forests also declare solid fuel fire bans, during which only gas appliances may be used, with a maximum penalty of $2,200. When forest fires are allowed, keep them under one square metre and 4.5 metres from the nearest log, stump or tree, with 2 metres of ground cleared around them.
Danger period 1 Oct to 31 Mar
Ban-day fire: $2,200 fine
Visitor gas generally banned in parks on ban days

Free camping in NSW mostly means state forests, plus national park campgrounds with no camping fee, most of which still charge a $6 booking fee. Camping is generally not allowed in state forest picnic areas, except at rest areas where highways pass through a forest.

Dogs are welcome in all state forests but must be under your control at all times, and Forestry Corporation asks that they stay on a lead. They are not allowed in most national parks, though some regional parks, such as Murrumbidgee Valley Regional Park, accept them, and many forests border national parks.
Councils decide where camping is banned on their land, and many ban it in beachfront car parks, so check the signs and the council's rules before staying overnight.

NSW marine parks have sanctuary zones where fishing is banned, and the zones are shown on the official zoning maps and in the FishSmart NSW app, because boundaries are not always obvious from the shore.

Beach driving is allowed only on some NSW beaches, and the rules vary: some need a council beach permit, some national park beaches need a park pass, and Worimi Conservation Lands near Port Stephens needs its own vehicle access permit, which annual park passes do not cover.
Many coastal campgrounds sit inside national parks, so the 21-day limit, the no-dogs rule and NPWS fire bans apply even where the beach feels like public land.
Check NPWS park alerts on the morning you travel, because coastal parks close roads after storms and campgrounds after fire or flood damage.

camping-rules-northern-territory.en: Camping Rules Northern Territory 2026: Passes & Free Camps
NT park camps are booked online at $10 to $20 per adult a night, and visitors need an NT Parks Visitor Pass. Free camping: signed 24-hour rest stops only.

Mostly no: Northern Territory parks allow camping only in marked areas that you book and pay for online, visitors also need an NT Parks Visitor Pass for most parks, and the free option is a roadside rest stop signed for 24-hour overnight camping. AussieCamps maps 102 NT park campgrounds and 23 public dump points, a thin network that makes every booked night count.

Designated campsites in NT parks, and the Jatbula, Larapinta and Tabletop tracks, are booked and paid for online, and rangers cannot take payment on site. Display the camping tag on your vehicle or tent, ready to show a ranger.

Visitors from outside the Territory need an NT Parks Visitor Pass for most parks and reserves, bought online before you go: $10 for a day, $30 for two weeks or $60 a year per adult. It does not cover Kakadu or Uluru-Kata Tjuta, which sell their own passes through Parks Australia.

Camping outside a designated campground needs a permit, with a fee of $4 per adult. Garig Gunak Barlu on the Cobourg Peninsula has its own permit, $232.10 per vehicle for up to five adults and seven nights, paid at least six weeks ahead, and the park opens only in the dry season.

Some campgrounds (Category C) are run by commercial operators, who set their own fees and handle bookings and payment themselves, so check with the operator before you go. Pets are generally not allowed in NT parks. Dogs can be walked at a few Darwin-area parks such as Casuarina Coastal Reserve and Holmes Jungle Nature Park, and near Alice Springs they may camp with you at Redbank Waterhole campground in Owen Springs Reserve.
Off-campground permit: $4 an adult
Garig Gunak Barlu: $232.10 a vehicle
No pets in most parks

Parks can close at short notice for flooding or bushfire, and most campgrounds stay open all year unless the season shuts them. Check the park page and the NT Road Report before every leg, even when it is dry where you are standing.
Saltwater crocodiles can be in any Top End waterway, so swim only where a sign says it is safe and camp at least 50 metres from the water.

Large areas of the Territory are Aboriginal land, and entering it needs a permit from the relevant land council. In the Top End that is the Northern Land Council, which warns that unauthorised entry can bring a fine of 50 penalty units, currently $18,200, under Commonwealth law.

An entry permit covers entry only: fishing or camping must be written into it. Main access roads into major communities need no permit, and the Mereenie Loop uses the Mereenie Tour Pass, free from the Central Land Council in Alice Springs, with no camping allowed along the loop.
Alcohol is banned in most Aboriginal communities unless a permit allows it. Check the rules for every community on your route before travelling with any in the vehicle.

Litchfield, Nitmiluk, Watarrka, Tjoritja / West MacDonnell and Judbarra / Gregory all need the NT Parks Visitor Pass. Kakadu needs a Parks Australia pass instead, valid for seven days: $25 per adult in the tropical summer (1 November to 14 May) and $40 in the dry season (15 May to 31 October), although visits from 1 July to 31 October 2026 are also charged the $25 rate. NT residents enter free.
The Jim Jim and Twin Falls area, including Karnamarr campground, is closed for all of 2026. Check the Kakadu access report, which is updated daily, before planning a day around any site.

NT park camping fees follow campground categories: $10 per adult at Category B sites, $15 at Category A and $20 at Category D, with lower child and family rates. Category C campgrounds are run commercially and set their own prices.

Saltwater crocodiles live in rivers, creeks, billabongs, estuaries and along the coast across the Top End, and the Territory says it is never completely safe to enter the water. Assume every waterway holds one.
Swimming areas open and close with surveys and water levels, so check the sign and the park page on the day rather than trusting a previous visit or an old guidebook.
Saltwater crocodiles live in fresh water as well as salt water, so a freshwater river or billabong is no guarantee of safety. Keep children well back from the bank and supervise them near water.

The Territory's own calendar runs the dry season from May to September, the build-up from October to December, the wet from January to mid-March and the run-off through March and April. Park campgrounds are busiest from May to September.

Heavy rain and road and park closures can run from November to April, while the waterfalls are at full flow. Some travellers prefer that season, but it means checking every park and road before you commit.
Central Australia swings between extremes. Temperatures can pass 40 degrees between October and April, and winter nights are cold, so pack for a hot afternoon and a cold night in the same day.

A fire ban usually lasts up to 24 hours. During one you must not start a fire in the open air, although a small cooking fire is allowed if it burns only while cooking, has 4 metres cleared around it and is always attended, and gas or coal barbecues can still be used.

Outside a ban, small fires for cooking and boiling water need no permit, but the 4 m clearing is still the law, with a maximum penalty of $15,000. Lighting a fire for any other purpose without a permit carries up to $77,000 or five years in prison.
Recreational fishing has bag and size limits, and some barramundi waters close for part of the year. Check the current NT fishing rules for the river you plan to fish.
Plants and animals in NT parks are protected, so leave rocks, plants and artefacts where they are, and gather firewood outside the park from fallen branches only.

In NT parks you book and pay for a campsite online and, as a visitor, also hold an NT Parks Visitor Pass. Camping outside a designated campground needs its own permit, and entering Aboriginal land needs a land council permit arranged before you go.

Many Top End campgrounds and unsealed roads close during the wet and run-off, roughly November to April, and parks can close at short notice for flooding or fire. Garig Gunak Barlu opens only in the dry season, and Kakadu's Jim Jim and Twin Falls area is closed for all of 2026.

camping-rules-queensland.en: Camping Rules Queensland 2026: Permits, Free Camps & Fees
No free camping in Queensland parks or forests: permits cost $7.75 a person a night in 2026. Free options are council sites; rest areas allow 20 hours.

Not in Queensland's parks or forests, where every camp needs a paid permit: $7.75 per person or $31 per family a night in 2026. Free camping means council campgrounds that allow it, and roadside rest areas let you stop for up to 20 hours unless a sign says otherwise, though the state says they are not camping sites. AussieCamps maps 517 Queensland park and forest campgrounds, 1,688 roadside rest areas and 324 public dump points.

You must book and pay for a camping permit before you arrive, online through the Queensland National Parks Booking Service, at a booking office or on 13 QGOV (13 74 68). Bookings open 12 months ahead, and the most popular spots are worth booking at least six weeks out.

Once camp is up, display the camping tag or your permit details on the tent, camping structure or vehicle dashboard. Without a printer, write the permit number, camping area, dates, number of people, surname and registration on paper in a clear weatherproof bag.

Bush camping is allowed only in some parks. Camp well away from streams, lakes, walking tracks and picnic areas, and where there are no toilets bury human waste at least 50 cm deep and 50 metres from water, tracks and camps.

If you drive in the recreation areas on K'gari, Bribie Island, Mulgumpin (Moreton Island), Minjerribah (North Stradbroke Island) or at Cooloola, you need a vehicle access permit as well as your camping permit. K'gari, Bribie and Cooloola permits can be booked together in the Queensland National Parks Booking Service, and number-plate cameras there mean the vehicle permit no longer has to be displayed.
Bush camp well away from water

Check Queensland park alerts, Bureau of Meteorology warnings and local fire bans before leaving. Queensland does not use the term Total Fire Ban: the Queensland Fire Department declares local fire bans for all or part of a council area, and they cover parks and forests.

Campfires are allowed only in camping areas that permit them, in existing QPWS fireplaces, fire rings or fire locations, with wood you bring in, and never during a fire ban or a QPWS fire prohibition. Gas and spirit stoves can still be used during a fire ban if they cannot throw embers, are contained and are never left unattended.

The camping fee from 1 July 2026 is $7.75 per person per night, or $31 per family, meaning one or two adults with children under 18, up to eight people. Children under five camp free, and fees rise slightly every July or August.

The permit system covers about 525 camping areas across Queensland's parks and forests, and none of them has electricity. You must reach your site within 24 hours of the permit start and must not leave it unattended for more than 24 hours.

Camping without a permit, or with more people than it covers, carries a maximum penalty of 20 penalty units. Rangers do issue on-the-spot fines: a group of four at Main Range National Park was fined $322 in 2025 for holding a one-person permit.
$7.75 per person a night
Families $31, under-fives free
Head counts are checked

Estuarine crocodiles live between Gladstone and Cape York Peninsula and throughout the Gulf of Carpentaria, in any waterway and the sea, including freshwater rivers, lagoons and swamps far inland. Obey every crocodile warning sign.

Set up camp well away from the water's edge, because crocodiles have attacked people in tents pitched too close to it. Do not swim or wade in croc country, stay at least 5 metres back from the water's edge, and do not clean fish there.

Report crocodile sightings to the Queensland environment department. Every report is investigated under the Queensland Crocodile Management Plan, and crocodiles that pose a threat to people are targeted for removal.

Queensland's cyclone season officially runs from 1 November to 30 April, and communities within 50 km of the coast from Bundaberg to Thursday Island and around the Gulf are the most exposed. Even a category 1 cyclone can damage caravans.
Wet-season rain closes unsealed roads and creek crossings quickly. Check park alerts, QLDTraffic and Bureau of Meteorology warnings every day, and never drive into floodwater.

En saison des pluies, routes et passages à gué peuvent fermer très vite.

camping-rules-queensland.en: The dry season, roughly May to October, is the best time for far northern camping, but many Cape York parks stay closed into June or July after the wet. Popular sites fill quickly in school and public holidays, so book at least six weeks ahead.

Free camping in Queensland means council-approved sites, not parks. Rest areas allow general and recreational vehicles to stop for up to 20 hours unless signed otherwise, but the state says they are not camping sites, and heavy-vehicle rest areas are for truck drivers only.

Councils set their own rules, and some run low-cost campgrounds or allow short stays at signed sites, so check the council's website first. Cities are stricter: Cairns bans camping on council land including roadsides, the Esplanade, parks, car parks and beaches.

Camping on a state-controlled road is illegal unless you are managing fatigue between 4pm and 8am, on a road that is not a motorway or toll road, where no sign bans it, outside a built-up area and at least 200 metres from any kerb or footpath. Fires, generators and detached trailers are not allowed, and rest areas ban generators between 7pm and 7am.
Rest areas: 20 hours unless signed

Always walk in groups on K'gari, because walking or sitting alone outside a fenced area makes a dingo encounter more likely. Families with children under 14 are strongly advised to camp in a fenced campground.
Never store food in your tent, and do not bring food or picnic on the lake shore or beach. Fines of up to $28,495 apply to anyone who disturbs or harms dingoes on K'gari.

Dogs and other pets are not allowed in Queensland national parks, though some conservation parks, state forests and recreation areas accept them. You may drive through a national park with a dog only on gazetted roads, with the dog inside the vehicle and without stopping at day-use areas, lookouts or other sites.
Drones are banned in every camping area in Queensland's protected areas, recreation areas and forests, so keep the drone stored in a container in your vehicle.

Yes. Every camp in a Queensland national park, state forest or recreation area needs a permit booked and paid for before you arrive, $7.75 per person or $31 per family a night in 2026, and the tag or permit details must be displayed at camp.

Not in parks or forests, which all charge. Free camping means council campgrounds that allow it. Roadside rest areas let you stop for up to 20 hours unless a sign says otherwise, but the state says they are not camping sites, and many coastal councils, including Cairns, ban camping on council land.

camping-rules-south-australia.en: Camping Rules South Australia 2026: Free Camps, Parks & Fees
Free camp on SA Crown land for up to 21 days; book national park campsites before you arrive. 2026 fees, fire season dates, fruit fly rules and fines.

Yes, you can free camp in South Australia, but only where the land manager allows it: Crown land allows camping for up to 21 days without approval, councils set the rules for their own reserves, and almost every national park campsite must be booked before you arrive, the Simpson Desert parks being the exception. AussieCamps maps 115 South Australian park campgrounds, 391 roadside rest areas and 199 public dump points.

Almost every South Australian national park campsite must be booked before arrival, online or through a booking agent, and bookings open up to 12 months ahead; the Munga-Thirri-Simpson Desert parks use the Desert Parks Pass instead. Check how many vehicles a site takes and its facilities before paying, because sites are priced by both.

A campground booking usually covers vehicle entry to that park, with Flinders Chase on Kangaroo Island the main exception. Keep the confirmation on your phone, and expect parks in the affected district to close on catastrophic fire danger days even when you hold a booking.

Collecting firewood is banned in South Australian parks, so bring clean, untreated wood where fires are allowed and use the pit provided. Ikara-Flinders Ranges bans wood fires from 15 October 2026 to 24 March 2027, and inside Wilpena Pound itself wood, solid-fuel and gas fires are banned all year, except gas at Wilcolo Camp.

Most national parks do not allow dogs or other pets, and Ikara-Flinders Ranges is one of them. Some parks allow dogs on a lead no longer than two metres; the park page says which, and a lead does not override a no-pets rule.
Bring firewood, never collect it
Ikara wood-fire ban to 24 March 2027
Most parks are pet-free

Outback tracks and desert park roads close after rain, often for days and, after major floods, for months. Check the park alert and the outback road report from the Department for Infrastructure and Transport before leaving the bitumen, and never drive around a closed sign.
Carry more water and fuel than the distance suggests, plus a way to call for help where there is no mobile coverage, such as a satellite messenger or a personal locator beacon.

Park entry and camping are separate products. A Multiple Entry Parks Pass covers vehicle entry only, as a single-park pass for 12 months or a multi-park pass for two or 12 months, and camping is still booked on top; the Desert Parks Pass is the exception and includes camping.

Most South Australian parks are free to enter. Where a day fee applies it is usually charged per vehicle, such as $14.40 at Ikara-Flinders Ranges, while Flinders Chase on Kangaroo Island charges each person instead.

Bookings open 12 months ahead, so book school holidays and long weekends as soon as your dates are fixed. Ikara-Flinders Ranges campsites start at $12.30 a night, while the powered sites and permanent tents at Wilpena are run by Wilpena Pound Resort rather than the parks booking system.
Entry passes don't include camping
Most parks are free to enter
Bookings open 12 months ahead

Travellers cannot bring fruit fly host fruit and vegetables, or some plants and plant products, into South Australia. The list depends on the state you are coming from, and a receipt does not make produce legal.

PIRSA checks vehicles at quarantine stations such as Yamba on the Sturt Highway and at random roadblocks, and from 1 July 2026 the fine for carrying restricted produce is up to $423. Eat or bin it before the border, because there is no disposal at Yamba itself, and restock from a shop once across.

The Riverland has its own controls inside the state. Buy fruit and vegetables there from accredited retailers rather than roadside stalls or markets, and check the current outbreak restrictions before a Murray River leg.
No restricted fruit over the border
Fines up to $423 from July 2026
Riverland: buy from accredited shops

The Desert Parks Pass gives 12 months of vehicle entry and camping in the far north: Innamincka Regional Reserve, Kati Thanda-Lake Eyre, Malkumba-Coongie Lakes, Munga-Thirri-Simpson Desert, Tallaringa and Witjira, plus entry only to Wabma Kadarbu Mound Springs, where camping is not allowed.

It is mandatory only for the Munga-Thirri-Simpson Desert National Park and Regional Reserve and for travel east of Dalhousie Springs in Witjira, and the Simpson Desert parks close every year from 1 December to 15 March. Elsewhere in the desert parks you can pay day entry and camping fees instead.

On the Oodnadatta, Strzelecki and Birdsville tracks, carry spare parts and two spare tyres, extra water and fuel for delays, and a satellite phone, beacon or UHF radio. Mobile reception is often unreliable once you leave town.

South Australia's Fire Danger Season is set by district. In 2026-27 it starts on 15 October in the Flinders, Eastern Eyre, West Coast and pastoral districts and on 1 November in the South East, Murraylands and Riverland, and runs into April. During it a campfire must sit in a trench 30 cm deep and no more than one square metre, with 4 m cleared around and above it, and a responsible person present at all times with water or an extinguisher.

On a Total Fire Ban day campfires and solid-fuel barbecues are banned. National parks go further and also ban gas and liquid-fuel stoves on those days and may close, so a gas cooker is no workaround inside a park.
Many parks ban wood fires at any time of year, and ForestrySA bans fires in its forests from 1 November to 30 April. Pack a gas cooker and plan meals that never depend on a fire.

Coorong beach camping needs a permit for each vehicle, is 4WD only and allows one vehicle with up to five people per site. The ocean beach between Tea Tree Crossing and the Murray Mouth closes to vehicles from 24 October to 24 December for nesting birds.

Many conservation parks do not allow camping at all; where they do, camp only at designated sites booked before you arrive. Coastal parks keep vehicles off the dunes, so stay on hard sand and marked tracks.

Crown land is one free alternative to a booked park. Camping there is allowed without approval for up to 21 days, vehicles must stay on established tracks, firewood collection is banned, and misuse can bring a $315 expiation.

Check the park alert on the morning you travel. Fire danger and track closures change quickly over summer, and some arid parks close for the whole season, such as Munga-Thirri-Simpson Desert from 1 December to 15 March.

camping-rules-tasmania.en: Camping Rules Tasmania 2026: Free Camps, Parks Pass & Fires
Free camp in Tasmania at signed council sites, free park camps and forestry land. 2026 Parks Pass prices, new camp fees from 3 November and fire rules.

Yes, you can free camp in Tasmania: at council sites that allow it, at free Parks and Wildlife Service campgrounds such as Huon and Teds Beach in Southwest National Park, and on most Sustainable Timber Tasmania land unless a sign prohibits it. Inside national parks you need a Parks Pass, campground fees come on top, and both bookings and fees change on 3 November 2026. AussieCamps maps 27 Tasmanian park campgrounds and 80 public dump points.

A valid parks pass is required to enter any Tasmanian national park, whether you arrive by car, on foot, by bus or by bike, and campground fees are paid on top. Free campsites inside a park, such as the Freycinet walker camps, still need the pass.

Parks and Wildlife Service moves to a new Parks Online Booking System on 3 November 2026 and has paused new bookings for stays from that date at campgrounds including Fortescue Bay and Richardsons Beach at Freycinet. Check when bookings reopen before fixing ferry dates around one site.

Council camping sites set their own conditions. Northern Midlands Council issues a free permit for self-contained vehicles to stay up to 48 hours. Central Coast Council allows up to three nights for self-contained vehicles, but it is moving its sites to a paid permit of $15 a night, so check the signs at each site rather than an old review.

On reserved land you must not camp in a designated camping-prohibited area or within 500 metres of a road outside a designated camping area, with a fine of up to 20 penalty units. Sustainable Timber Tasmania welcomes camping on the land it manages except where signs prohibit it.
Council limits vary: check each sign

Tasmanian weather turns fast, and severe cold, wet and windy conditions can arrive at any time of year, even in summer. Pack for cold rain in January and move off exposed camps when the Bureau of Meteorology issues a severe weather warning for damaging winds.
Clean boots, bikes and camping gear before moving between walks and waterways, so soil, seeds and water pests do not travel with you into the wilderness.

Prices from 1 July 2026: a daily pass costs $49.15 per vehicle carrying up to eight people, or $24.55 per person on foot, bus or bike, and it does not cover Cradle Mountain. The holiday pass covers every national park for up to two months for $98.35 per vehicle, and the annual pass costs $104.75.
Two daily passes cost about the same as one holiday pass, so it pays from the third day of park visits. Buy it online at passes.parks.tas.gov.au before you travel.

Cradle Mountain runs a shuttle from the visitor centre, and private vehicles cannot drive into the park while it operates. The Cradle Mountain daily pass costs $30.70 per adult and includes the shuttle; holiday pass holders buy a shuttle ticket separately.
Holiday pass: $98.35 for two months
Daily pass excludes Cradle Mountain

Tasmania has strict biosecurity rules, and fresh fruit and vegetables are among the items you cannot bring in. X-ray machines and detector dogs screen arrivals at Hobart and Launceston airports.

On the Spirit of Tasmania you can eat your own food on board, but leftovers go in the bins on board or at the biosecurity inspection point as you leave the terminal. Staff at Geelong ask biosecurity questions before boarding, and Biosecurity Tasmania runs random vehicle checks at Devonport.

Penalties apply to restricted items that are not declared, and the rules protect an island that is free of several pests found on the mainland. Eat or bin fresh food before you sail and restock in Devonport.

Walks above the treeline are alpine outings whatever the forecast at the car park says. Cold, wet and windy weather can arrive in any month on the high plateaus, including in the middle of summer.
Carry warm and waterproof layers on every walk, including in January. Hypothermia develops quickly in wind and rain, even on a short walk from the car.

Huon and Teds Beach in Southwest National Park take no bookings and charge no camping fee, and Freycinet's Wineglass Bay, Hazards and Cooks Beach walker camps and Encampment Cove on Maria Island are also free to camp. The parks pass still applies inside each park.

Other park campgrounds are booked or first come depending on the season. Fortescue Bay takes bookings from 1 October to 30 April and is first in, first served from May to September, and from 3 November 2026 it charges $24 a site for up to six people.
The west coast is wet, remote and thinly serviced. Fill up and shop in Queenstown or Strahan, because the gaps between towns on that side of the island are long.

The Overland Track needs a booking and a fee from 1 October to 31 May: $312 per adult, with lower fees for children and concession holders, walking north to south only. Bookings open on the first Tuesday in July, and the fee includes park entry for the walk and the shuttle.
Outside the booking season, from June to September, there is no Overland Track fee, but you still need a parks pass, must register your walk online with PWS and need full winter gear.

Fuel Stove Only Areas ban campfires all year across much of the wilderness, including Cradle Mountain-Lake St Clair, Freycinet, Mount Field, Southwest and the Walls of Jerusalem, whatever the fire danger rating. A few marked sites in the World Heritage Area and Tasman National Park allow fires in existing fireplaces.

On a Total Fire Ban day all outdoor fires are banned in parks. LPG and electric stoves are the only exceptions, methylated spirits and shellite stoves are not allowed, and Freycinet bans every naked flame in the open, gas included.

camping-rules-victoria.en: Camping Rules Victoria 2026: Free Camping, Forests & Fees
Free camp in Victorian state forests for up to 28 nights, 20 m from water. Bookable Parks Victoria camps are half price until July 2027. 2026 fire rules.

Yes, you can free camp in Victoria: state forests let you camp almost anywhere for up to 28 consecutive nights if you stay at least 20 metres from waterways, every state forest campground is free except Murrindindi Scenic Reserve, and some Parks Victoria campgrounds charge nothing and take no bookings. AussieCamps maps 438 Victorian campgrounds, 350 of them state forest and Crown land sites managed by DEECA and 88 run by Parks Victoria, plus 651 roadside rest areas and 181 public dump points.

Bookable Parks Victoria campgrounds need a booking made in advance with your vehicle registration. You no longer have to print or display the permit, but make sure the car registration on your booking is correct; you can update it at any time through 'manage booking' in the confirmation email.

Some park campgrounds are free with no booking, such as Warby-Ovens National Park and King Hut in the Alpine National Park, while others open only in certain seasons: Lake Catani at Mount Buffalo is closed from 31 August to 30 October 2026. Don't take a booked or closed site just because it looks empty.

State forests run on different rules from national parks. You can camp anywhere in a state forest at least 20 metres from a waterway for no more than 28 consecutive nights, but in forest reserves you must use the campgrounds the land manager provides.

Rest areas are built for rest breaks, not camping. Those on major roads are run by Transport Victoria and councils set overnight rules on local roads, so follow the signs at each stop and don't stay overnight unless a sign allows it.
Forest: 20 m from water
28 consecutive nights at most
Forest reserves: campgrounds only

Fire conditions in Victoria change from day to day, and on Total Fire Ban days fires are more likely to spread quickly. Check the VicEmergency app and the park alert page every morning in summer, and never light a fire when restrictions prohibit it.
Alpine and forest roads close for winter and after storms. Respect locked gates, and keep a lower-altitude campground in reserve in case the high country turns you back.

Camping fees at 131 bookable Parks Victoria campgrounds have been half price since 1 July 2025, and the Victorian Government has funded that until July 2027. The earlier free-camping scheme at those campgrounds ended on 30 June 2025, so a booking and a fee still apply.

Peak season at Wilsons Promontory is handled through quarterly booking releases, not a ballot. Tidal River bookings for 1 March to 30 June 2027 opened on 28 September 2026, and over the summer peak, 20 December 2026 to 24 January 2027, campsites need a 7-night minimum stay arriving and leaving on a Sunday. Since 1 July 2026 some Great Ocean Road campsites are booked through the Great Ocean Road Coast and Parks Authority.

One booking can now hold up to three campsites in the same campground. Most sites include one vehicle in the fee and Tidal River allows two cars per site, so check the limit on the booking before you bring a second car or trailer.

No Wilsons Prom ballot

Victoria's state forests have more than 300 campgrounds, and all of them are free except Murrindindi Scenic Reserve, where a small permit fee applies. There are no facilities at informal sites, so bring water, a shovel and every bag of rubbish back out.

Dig toilet holes at least 30 cm deep and 100 metres from any waterway, and tip washing-up water at least 50 metres from rivers and creeks. Building anything permanent or semi-permanent needs a permit.

Seasonal road closures run from June to November each year to protect tracks that are easily damaged when wet. In 2026 most closures in Parks Victoria parks started on 4 or 11 June and lifted on 29 October; check the FFMVic closures map for state forest roads, and expect a fine for driving a closed road.

The Fire Danger Period starts and ends at different dates in each council area, usually before summer and lasting until April or May. For 2026-27 it began on 5 October in East Gippsland and Wellington.

In a state forest, use a purpose-built fireplace if you can, either a site firepit or a portable one, keep the fire under one metre across with three metres cleared around it, and never leave it unattended. During the Fire Danger Period the fire must be in a stone, metal or concrete fireplace or a trench at least 30 cm deep, and in national and state parks you may only use the fireplaces the park provides.

On a Total Fire Ban day, campfires and barbecues or stoves that burn solid or chemical fuel are banned across every district the ban covers, and some bans cover the whole state. CFA warns that lighting a fire on one of those days can bring a fine of more than $40,000, two years in prison, or both.

Some coastal councils are strict. Surf Coast Shire, which covers Torquay, Anglesea and Lorne, makes sleeping in a vehicle anywhere in the shire an offence with a $300 on-the-spot fine, so don't sleep in your vehicle in any car park or street there; book a caravan park or campground instead.
Some inland councils run free or low-cost camping areas, and some showgrounds take campers. Check the council website or ask at the visitor centre for the current arrangement.

Wilsons Promontory bans pets, drones, generators, campfires and solid-fuel barbecues, and dogs are generally not allowed in Victorian national parks. State forests are the dog-friendly alternative, with dogs on a lead or under control around camps and facilities.

On the Bogong High Plains, dispersed camping is not allowed within 200 metres of the Bogong High Plains or Pretty Valley roads. Firewood is scarce up high, so Parks Victoria asks campers to use a stove.

On licensed Crown river frontages, often grazed by the neighbouring farm, you may camp only in designated areas, for up to 14 nights, more than 20 metres from the water and 200 metres from a house, and without dogs. On unlicensed Crown frontages you can camp more than 20 metres from the water and 200 metres from a house for up to 28 consecutive nights.
Parks Victoria publishes the seasonal road closure list each year, and reading it before planning a High Country loop saves a wasted drive to a locked gate.

camping-rules-western-australia.en: Camping Rules Western Australia 2026: Free Camps & Fees
Free camping in WA means signed rest stops for up to 24 hours or approved sites. Park camps cost $10 to $20 per adult a night. 2026 passes, fires, permits.

Only in limited places: Western Australia lets you camp outside a licensed caravan park or camping ground only with approval, and the main free exception is a signed overnight rest stop, where you can stay up to 24 consecutive hours. In national parks you camp only in designated campgrounds, at $10 to $20 per adult a night. AussieCamps maps 260 Western Australian park campgrounds and 238 public dump points across those long distances.

Many national park campgrounds are booked through Park Stay WA, up to 180 days ahead. Fees are per person per night: $10 an adult at campgrounds without facilities, $15 with basic facilities and $20 with additional facilities, and children aged 5 and under camp free.

Campgrounds that cannot be booked are first come, first served, and sites are usually available outside the busiest periods, but vacancies are not guaranteed. Fees are still payable, usually in cash or by self-registration envelope. Arrive early and keep a legal alternative within your fuel range.

Main Roads WA says its 24-hour rest areas are not intended for camping, a stay must not exceed 24 consecutive hours, and no overnight stop is allowed at a rest area without a sign permitting it. Keep heavy-vehicle bays clear for road trains.

Camping anywhere else outside a licensed caravan park or camping ground without approval risks an offence, whether the land is public or private. On private land, the owner's permission covers a stay of up to 5 nights; longer stays also need local government approval. Some local governments run their own designated sites.
24 consecutive hours at most
Only where a sign allows it
Elsewhere needs approval

Most park campgrounds have no drinking water. Where rainwater or bore water is available, supply is not guaranteed and you should boil, treat or filter it, so carry all the water you need. In national parks, fires are allowed only in the fire rings provided, with at least three metres cleared around them, and restrictions can start without notice.

Collecting firewood, even dead wood, is banned in national parks, nature reserves and conservation parks. In State forest it is allowed only in designated firewood areas in the Perth Hills (with a permit) and the South West, so bring firewood or buy it near where you will burn it. Many parks stop campfires from about 1 December to 31 March, and some never allow them.
Western Australia covers about a third of the continent, and the gaps between parks, towns and fuel shape every camping plan. A full or closed campground can cost a day of driving.

Park entry is charged separately from camping at parks such as Karijini and Cape Range: $17 per standard vehicle, or $10 with a concession. The All Parks Pass costs $130 a year ($80 concession) and holiday passes start at $30, so a pass pays off quickly on a run up the coast.
Northern roads and campgrounds follow the weather rather than the calendar. Check DBCA park alerts and the Main Roads WA Travel Map before each leg, and ask the local shire about shire-managed roads.
Karijini entry: $17 a vehicle
All Parks Pass: $130 a year

Outside paid campgrounds, the main place the state lets you stay overnight without approval is a signed overnight rest stop, for up to 24 consecutive hours. Main Roads WA treats that limit as one to enforce, and the official rules allow no longer stays at roadside sites.

Some local governments run low-cost or free campgrounds for travellers, each with its own stay limit and conditions. Ask the shire or the visitor centre, because the rules change from one shire to the next.

Station stays, where pastoral properties open camping areas to travellers, are a distinctive WA option, and some make a handy stopover on long remote stretches, such as Cheela Plains between Ningaloo and Karijini. Confirm the price, payment method and road access with the station before you arrive.

Ningaloo Coast campgrounds release bookings monthly, on the first Tuesday at 10am Perth time, a system adopted in September 2026 after an eight-month trial. Stays are capped at 14 nights if any night falls in WA school holidays and 28 nights otherwise.

Severe Tropical Cyclone Narelle damaged every campground along the Ningaloo Coast in 2026. Most Cape Range campgrounds reopened on 27 April but some stayed closed for longer, so check the alert for your exact site.

The north works best in the dry season, roughly May to October, and the cyclone season runs from November to April. Inland summer temperatures regularly pass 40 degrees, and a breakdown in that heat without water is life-threatening.

Dogs and other pets are not allowed in many national parks, including Karijini and Cape Range. Plan pet-friendly stops between them before you set off.

A caravan park and a holiday park are much the same thing: commercial parks with powered sites, amenities and usually cabins, with holiday parks leaning towards pools, playgrounds and family facilities. A campground in a national park or state forest trades those services for the setting and a lower fee or none. Match the stay to what the trip needs that night rather than using one type for the whole route.
Caravan park or holiday park: what the names mean

The two names overlap and operators use them loosely. Both describe a commercial park with powered and unpowered sites, amenities blocks and usually cabins; holiday park tends to signal more family facilities such as a pool, a playground or activities, and often more cabins.

The bigger difference is between commercial parks and public campgrounds. Parks sell services, power and convenience, while national park and forest campgrounds sell the location and leave most of the services to you.

is-free-camping-legal-australia.en: Is Free Camping Legal in Australia? Rules by State 2026
is-free-camping-legal-australia.oldEn: Is free camping legal in Australia?

is-free-camping-legal-australia.en: Free camping is legal only where the land manager allows it: state forests, some council sites and signed rest areas. The rules in every state for 2026.

Yes, but only where the land manager allows it: there is no national right to camp wherever a vehicle can park. Free camping is legal in most state forests in New South Wales and Victoria, on South Australian Crown land for up to 21 days, at council sites that say so and at rest areas whose rules allow an overnight stop. Most national park campgrounds charge a fee or need a booking, and some coastal councils, such as Surf Coast Shire in Victoria, fine people for sleeping in a vehicle.
Where free camping is legal: the eastern states

In New South Wales every state forest except Cumberland and Strickland allows free, first-come camping for up to four weeks. Some national park campgrounds charge no camping fee but still need a booking, which costs $6.

Victoria lets you camp almost anywhere in a state forest for up to 28 consecutive nights, at least 20 metres from waterways, and a few Parks Victoria campgrounds such as King Hut are free with no booking.

Queensland has no free camping in its parks or state forests, where every campsite needs a paid permit. The free options there are council campgrounds that allow it. Roadside rest areas let you stop for up to 20 hours unless a sign says otherwise, but the state says they are not camping sites.

Tasmania offers free council camps with their own permits and stay limits, free park campgrounds in Southwest National Park (a parks pass is still needed to enter), and camping on most Sustainable Timber Tasmania land unless a sign prohibits it.

Can you camp on the side of the road?

Usually not, unless the spot is a rest area that allows it. Queensland bans camping on a state-controlled road unless you are managing fatigue between 4pm and 8am, outside a built-up area, at least 200 metres from any kerb and 9 metres from the traffic lane, where no sign prohibits it and not on a motorway or toll road, with no fire or generator.

Western Australia's Main Roads allows no overnight stop at a rest area without a sign permitting it, and Service NSW says rest areas are not for camping, although a July 2026 planning note says camping in one may be allowed unless a sign says otherwise.
Where an overnight stop is allowed, keep it to the vehicle, leave the truck bays free for heavy vehicles and move on in the morning.
Fines and how they are set

Penalties are set by whoever owns the land, so they vary widely. Camping outside a camping area in a NSW national park carries a maximum of 30 penalty units, the ACT sets a maximum of 20 penalty units ($3,200 for an individual) for using public land, including camping on it, without a permit, and misuse of South Australian Crown land can bring a $315 expiation.
Council fines are set locally, so the amount differs from one council to the next. Check the council's website or the sign at the site.

Some councils allow free camping only for self-contained vehicles with an onboard toilet and waste tanks. Each council defines what counts, so check its conditions before relying on a portable toilet.
Self-containment can open up more sites, but it does not lift the stay limit. The stay limit on the sign still applies, and waste still goes only into a dump point.

Yes, in the right place: what gets people fined is camping where it is banned, and many councils count sleeping in a parked car as camping. The legal options are booked campgrounds, state forests that allow camping, and rest areas whose rules or signs permit an overnight stop, such as Queensland's 20-hour limit and Western Australia's signed 24-hour stops.
The rules in each state

No state publishes one simple yes or no. Road authorities set rest-area limits, councils set the rules for streets, beaches and car parks, and park agencies decide what happens inside national parks, so the answer depends on which of the three owns the ground under your car.

Only Queensland and Western Australia publish a statewide rest-area time limit, and the Northern Territory lists which of its highway rest stops allow overnight camping. Everywhere else the sign at the rest area decides, and advice in New South Wales is mixed: Service NSW says rest areas are not for camping, while a July 2026 planning practice note says camping in one may be permitted unless a sign says otherwise.

Queensland lets general and recreational vehicles stay at a rest area for up to 20 hours unless a sign says otherwise, but calls them stopping places rather than campsites. Heavy-vehicle rest areas are for truck drivers only, and generators must stay off between 7pm and 7am.

In Western Australia you can stop for up to 24 consecutive hours at rest areas marked for overnight stays, which Main Roads WA says are not intended for camping, and you need approval to stay overnight anywhere else outside a caravan park or campground. The Northern Territory lists its road rest stops one by one, and only those marked for 24-hour overnight camping allow it.

Wherever you stop, park inside the marked bays, keep truck parking clear and leave the awning, chairs and table packed. A car with people asleep in it reads as a rest stop; a set-up camp reads as camping.

Councils, cities and the coast

Local laws are where most fines come from. On the Victorian coast, Surf Coast Shire treats sleeping in a vehicle anywhere in the shire as an offence with a $300 on-the-spot fine, and Cairns Regional Council bans camping on roadsides, the Esplanade, parks, car parks and beaches.

Some inland councils run free or low-cost areas for travellers. Tasmania's Northern Midlands Council, for example, issues free permits for stays of up to 48 hours, but only for fully self-contained vehicles with their own toilet and shower, which rules out most cars.
Read the sign for the exact bay, not just the street. Time limits, permit zones and no-overnight signs often sit side by side, and all of them apply at once.

Carbon monoxide, heat and cold

Never run the engine for heating or air conditioning while you sleep, and never bring a gas heater, cooker or barbecue inside. Western Australia's gas safety regulator warns that portable outdoor gas appliances must never be used inside a tent, semi-enclosed area, caravan, RV or indoors, because of the risk of carbon monoxide poisoning.
Summer heat is the main practical limit on sleeping in a car. Cabins heat quickly after sunrise and stay warm overnight in the north, so start the day early or choose a powered site with shade.
Inland and alpine nights fall below freezing in winter and a car holds little warmth. A sleeping bag rated for the conditions matters more in a vehicle than in a tent.
sleeping-in-car-australia.oldEn: In winter, inland and alpine nights drop below freezing and a car offers almost no insulation. A proper sleeping bag rated to the conditions matters more in a vehicle than in a tent.

Where a legal night is easiest

State forests are the simplest free option in New South Wales and Victoria, where camping is generally allowed for up to four weeks and 28 consecutive nights respectively. NSW forests do not allow camping in picnic areas, and in Victoria you must camp at least 20 metres from waterways.

South Australia allows camping on Crown land for up to 21 days without approval, while Western Australia expects you to use a licensed caravan park, a campground or a signed rest stop unless you have approval.
When in doubt, a basic campground or showground costs little and removes the question. Arrive before dark so you can read the signs and check the access for your vehicle.

towing-caravan-australia-road-rules.en: It depends on the state. Western Australia caps any vehicle towing a trailer or caravan at 100 km/h. In NSW the 100 km/h cap applies when the towing vehicle's GVM or GCM is over 4.5 tonnes; below that the posted limit applies. Check each state's towing rules before crossing a border, and drive to the rig's stability and the conditions.

A standard car licence covers a tow vehicle of up to 4.5 tonnes gross vehicle mass (GVM); a heavier vehicle needs a light rigid licence or higher. The licence does not raise towing limits: the loaded caravan must stay within the lowest of the vehicle's towing capacity, the towbar and coupling rating, the caravan's own rating and the tyres' load rating. In NSW, learners cannot tow and P1 drivers may only tow trailers up to 250 kg unladen.
